title: A person carrying a heavy bag in one hand often leans their body towards the opposite side. What is the main mechanical reason?
question: A person carrying a heavy bag in one hand often leans their body towards the opposite side. What is the main mechanical reason?

options.text: To reduce the gravitational field around the bag.
To shift the person's combined centre of gravity and maintain balance.
To increase the bag's mass temporarily.
To eliminate the normal reaction from the ground.

explanation:
?

A. To reduce the gravitational field around the bag.  
B. To shift the person's combined centre of gravity and maintain balance.  
C. To increase the bag's mass temporarily.  
D. To eliminate the normal reaction from the ground.

**Correct answer: B**

**Explanation:** Leaning shifts the combined centre of gravity of the person and bag so that its vertical line can remain within the base of support.

title: A hollow ring and a uniform solid disc have equal outer radii and are made of the same material. Which statement about their centres of gravity is correct?
question: A hollow ring and a uniform solid disc have equal outer radii and are made of the same material. Which statement about their centres of gravity is correct?

options.text: The ring's centre of gravity lies on its circumference.
The disc's centre of gravity lies below its geometric centre.
Both centres of gravity coincide with their respective geometric centres.
The ring has no centre of gravity because its centre is empty.

explanation: Both objects have symmetric mass distributions about their geometric centres. A centre of gravity does not need to contain any material.

title: A body is cut into two pieces, and one piece is removed. Which statement about the centre of gravity of the remaining body is correct?
question: A body is cut into two pieces, and one piece is removed. Which statement about the centre of gravity of the remaining body is correct?

options.text: It must remain at the original centre of gravity.
It must shift towards the removed piece.
Its new position depends on the remaining mass distribution.
It must lie outside the remaining body.

explanation: The centre of gravity depends on how mass is distributed. Removing a portion changes the distribution, so the new centre of gravity must be determined from the remaining shape and mass.

title: Which feature distinguishes a couple from a single force acting on a rigid body?
question: Which feature distinguishes a couple from a single force acting on a rigid body?

options.text: A couple always has a non-zero resultant force.
A couple consists of equal and opposite parallel forces acting along different lines.
A couple can only act vertically.

explanation: A couple has zero resultant force but a non-zero turning effect because its equal and opposite forces act along distinct parallel lines.

title: A couple acts on a freely movable rigid body. Which effect does it produce ideally?
question: A couple acts on a freely movable rigid body. Which effect does it produce ideally?

options.text: Rotation without a resultant force causing translation.
A change in mass without motion.

explanation: The net force of a couple is zero, so it does not produce linear acceleration of the centre of mass. Its non-zero moment can produce angular acceleration.

title: Two couples have equal moments but are formed using different force magnitudes. What must be true of them?
question: Two couples have equal moments but are formed using different force magnitudes. What must be true of them?

options.text: Their forces must have equal magnitudes.
Their perpendicular separations must be equal.
The product of force magnitude and perpendicular separation must be equal.
Their directions of rotation must be opposite.

explanation: The moment of a couple equals one force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. Equal moments require equal products, not necessarily equal forces or separations.

title: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum is located between the effort and the load. Which statement is correct?
question: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum is located between the effort and the load. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The effort arm must always be longer than the load arm.
The lever can change the direction of the applied effort.
The mechanical advantage must always be less than one.
The load must always lie vertically below the fulcrum.

explanation: A first-class lever can reverse the direction of effort. Its mechanical advantage depends on the relative lengths of the effort and load arms, so it may be less than, equal to or greater than one.

title: A second-class lever is generally capable of multiplying force because:
question: A second-class lever is generally capable of multiplying force because:

options.text: The fulcrum lies between the load and effort.
The effort arm is shorter than the load arm.
The load lies between the fulcrum and effort, making the effort arm longer than the load arm.

explanation: In a second-class lever, the load lies between the fulcrum and effort. The effort arm is longer than the load arm, giving a mechanical advantage greater than one in the ideal case.

title: A third-class lever is useful even though its mechanical advantage is usually less than one. Why?
question: A third-class lever is useful even though its mechanical advantage is usually less than one. Why?

options.text: It can provide a greater range or speed of movement of the load.
It eliminates the need for effort.

explanation: In a third-class lever, the effort lies between the fulcrum and load. The load moves through a greater distance and often at greater speed than the effort point, although a larger effort is generally needed.

title: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circular path. What would happen if this force suddenly disappeared?
question: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circular path. What would happen if this force suddenly disappeared?

options.text: The body would continue along the circular path.
The body would move along a tangent to the circle at the point of release.
The body would move radially outward in a straight line.

explanation: By Newton's first law, the body continues with its instantaneous velocity. That velocity is tangential to the circular path, so the body moves along the tangent if the centripetal force disappears.

title: A stone is tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle. The string provides the centripetal force. Which statement is correct?
question: A stone is tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle. The string provides the centripetal force. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The force acts along the direction of the stone's instantaneous velocity.
The force acts radially towards the centre and changes the direction of velocity.
The force acts radially outward and increases the speed continuously.
The force is absent because the speed is constant.

explanation: The centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circle and continually changes the direction of velocity. In ideal uniform circular motion, it does not change the speed.

title: A body is in equilibrium under three coplanar, non-parallel forces. Which statement gives the most appropriate condition for equilibrium?
question: A body is in equilibrium under three coplanar, non-parallel forces. Which statement gives the most appropriate condition for equilibrium?

options.text: All three forces must have equal magnitudes.
All three forces must act in the same direction.
Their vector sum must be zero, and their lines of action must be consistent with zero resultant moment.
The body must have zero mass.

explanation: Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment. For three coplanar forces that are non-parallel and in equilibrium, their lines of action must meet at a common point (or be concurrent).

title: The Same Speed, a Smaller Circle
question: A particle of mass m moves at constant speed v in a horizontal circular path of radius r under centripetal force F. If the radius is halved while the speed remains unchanged, what happens to the required centripetal force?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

    <text x="195" y="122" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Radius = 1 m</text>
    <text x="67" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Same speed</text>
  </svg>

options.text: It becomes four times as large.

explanation: Centripetal force F = (m × v²) / r. When mass m and speed v remain constant, F is inversely proportional to radius r (F ∝ 1/r). Halving the radius doubles the required centripetal force: F' / F = r / (r/2) = 2.

explanation:
F₁ and F₂ are perpendicular to the rod, so each produces a moment of magnitude


20×0.30=6 N m


But one tends to rotate the rod anticlockwise and the other clockwise.

F₃ is inclined at 45^°, so its moment magnitude is


20×0.30×sin45^°
≈4.24 N m


Thus F₁ and F₂ have equal magnitudes of moment but opposite turning directions.

**Concept tested:** Direction of moment and the perpendicular component of an inclined force.

title: The Weight of a Non-Uniform Metre Rule
question: A non-uniform metre rule balances horizontally on a knife edge at the 40 cm mark. A 30 N weight hangs at the 80 cm mark. The rule's weight acts at its centre of gravity, at an unknown position x. If the weight of the rule is 60 N, find x. Options
explanation:
The 30 N weight produces a clockwise moment:


30(80-40)=1200 N cm


For equilibrium, the rule's weight must act to the left of the pivot and produce an equal anticlockwise moment:


60(40-x)=1200



40-x=20Rightarrow x=20 cm


Therefore, the correct answer is actually **A. 20 cm**.

**Concept tested:** Locating the centre of gravity of a non-uniform body using moments.

title: The Lever with a Moving Fulcrum

diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="40" x2="300" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M78 84 L93 44 L108 84 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M148 84 L163 44 L178 84 Z" fill="none" stroke="#777" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><line x1="30" y1="40" x2="30" y2="72" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="30,79 24,67 36,67" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="17" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Load</text><line x1="270" y1="40" x2="270" y2="72" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="270,79 264,67 276,67" fill="#d97706" /><text x="252" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Effort</text><text x="73" y="106" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 1</text><text x="147" y="120" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 2</text></svg>

title: Metre Rule with Its Own Weight — Recurring ICSE Pattern
question: A metre rule of weight W balances on a knife edge at the 45 cm mark. A 20 N load is suspended at the 70 cm mark. Assuming the rule is uniform, what is its weight?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="40" width="290" height="12" rx="2" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" /><line x1="145" y1="52" x2="145" y2="89" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="145,96 139,84 151,84" fill="#2878c8" /><path d="M128 98 L145 56 L162 98 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="218" y1="52" x2="218" y2="84" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="218,91 212,79 224,79" fill="#d97706" /><text x="115" y="116" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot at 45 cm</text><text x="195" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Weight at 70 cm</text><text x="14" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0 cm</text><text x="267" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">100 cm</text></svg>
explanation:
Since the rule is uniform, its weight acts at the 50 cm mark.

Distance of the rule's weight from the pivot:


50-45=5 cm


Distance of the suspended load:


70-45=25 cm


Using the principle of moments:


W×5=20×25



W=(500 / 5)=100 N


Therefore, the correct answer is **not among the options**; the correct value is 100 N. This illustrates why the metre rule's own weight must be included in the moment calculation.

title: The Rod Suspended by Two Strings
question: A uniform horizontal rod weighing 120 N is suspended by two vertical strings attached symmetrically at its ends. A further 40 N weight is attached exactly at its centre. Find the tension in each string.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="20" x2="300" y2="20" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="65" y1="20" x2="65" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="255" y1="20" x2="255" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="35" y1="75" x2="285" y2="75" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" /><line x1="160" y1="75" x2="160" y2="116" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="160,123 154,111 166,111" fill="#d97706" /><text x="173" y="110" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">120 N</text><text x="42" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₁</text><text x="263" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₂</text></svg>

Total downward force:

120+40=160 N
